steps.observation: You have 10 seconds. Write a short story about a lighthouse keeper.

steps.action:
The storm came in sideways, a gray wall erasing sea and sky. Elias braced himself against the lantern room’s glass, feeling the old tower shudder as the wind howled around it like some hungry thing.

For forty-three years, he had kept this light. He knew the sea’s moods: the lazy summer roll of waves, the winter fury that tore at the rocks below. Tonight felt different—too sudden, too violent, as if the ocean had changed its mind about the land.

The bulb hummed behind him, the great lens turning with slow, patient dignity. White beams swept the chaos, carving corridors of clarity through rain and spray. Elias checked the mechanisms for the fifth time anyway. Habit was a comfort. Habit meant control.

Below, the radio crackled and spat, snatches of voices drowning in static.

“—lost rudder—drifting—no bearings—”

He grabbed the microphone. “This is Northpoint Light. I have you. I see you on the water—bearing zero-eight. Keep your bow toward the beam as it passes. You’re coming in close to the teeth.”

“The what?”

“The reef,” Elias said. “You don’t have room for a mistake.”

There was a pause, filled with wind’s hiss. “Sir, we’ve lost all instruments. We’re blind out here.”

“Then borrow my eyes,” Elias said. “Count with me. When the light hits you: one… two… three… turn starboard five degrees. Again when it comes around. Don’t think—just count and turn.”

He set the microphone down between sweeps, watching. Through the whipping rain he could just make out a dark shape rising and falling, far too near the boiling white where waves struck hidden stone.

The beam swung, caught the vessel: a small fishing boat, bow yawing, barely keeping its nose to safety. One… two… three… He could almost see the wheel turning under someone’s desperate hands.

“Good,” he muttered to no one. “Good. Again.”

For long minutes, their world shrank to a shared rhythm: the turning of the lens, the counting, the answering shift of the boat. The storm tried to tear them apart; the light stitched them together every eight seconds.

At last, between curtains of rain, he saw it: the narrow tongue of calmer water that led past the reef into the bay. He adjusted the timing of his counts, nudging them gently, unseen, between jagged shadows.

“You’ve cleared the teeth,” he said into the microphone. “Turn ten degrees port. You’ll find the harbor mouth dead ahead. You’ll see the town’s pier lights soon.”

The answer came, choked with relief. “We see them! God, we see them. Thank you, Northpoint. We would’ve— We couldn’t even tell which way was land.”

Elias allowed himself a small, private smile. “Land’s where it’s always been. Go on in. They’ll have hot coffee ready.”

He hung the microphone and leaned his forehead against the cool glass. Outside, the storm raged on, uncaring, dragging the world into a maelstrom of wind and noise. But in the midst of it, the lighthouse turned its steady circle, indifferent to gratitude, ignorant of fear.

People in town had said for years that lighthouses were obsolete now—GPS, computers, satellites. The budget meetings kept circling talk of automation, of darkness. Elias had attended them in his one good suit, hands folded, saying little.

The thing about satellites, he thought, listening to the radio’s empty hiss, is that they live above the weather. Up there, storms are shapes on screens. Down here, storms are hands on the door.

He went downstairs, checked the fuel, checked the spare bulb, checked the backup generators; then he climbed back up again to watch the sea. The boat’s small running lights disappeared behind the headland, safe. Another anonymous vessel, another set of lives he would never meet in daylight.

The wind screamed. The tower shook. The lens turned, unhurried and perfect.

Elias settled into his chair by the window, collar damp, joints aching. Outside, the world vanished and reappeared with each slow sweep of light: blackness, then foamed rock, then nothing again.

Alone on the cliff, with the storm clawing at the stone beneath him, the keeper stayed at his post, doing the one simple thing he knew how to do: when everything else failed, he kept the light turning.
